rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to reveal which crowded pairs respond to slope. All peaks should remain comfortably within the acquisition window.

The shallower gradient resolves all but one pair, so test temperature selectivity without changing the slope. Raising temperature may separate the remaining pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Slightly reduce the gradient slope at the best temperature to improve the remaining critical pair. The last peak has enough time margin that this extension should still keep elution below 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower slope, so shorten the gradient to move it away from co-elution. Monitor the early pair at R 1.61, which may lose some resolution as the gradient steepens.

The best method is just short of full resolution, with the limiting pair at R 1.46. Lower temperature by one step to tune selectivity while retaining the favorable gradient slope and ample margin below 10 minutes.

Return to 60 C and raise the starting organic fraction one step to adjust selectivity and slightly reduce gradient steepness. This tests whether the nearly resolved early pair can reach R 1.5 without sacrificing the later critical pair.

Use the narrower solvent window to obtain a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, slightly shallower than injection 7. This should improve both early critical pairs while preserving the later pair’s resolution margin and keeping all peaks within the gradient.

Injection 8 has reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter elution window. Raising phi0 one step should accelerate elution while the slightly shallower slope may preserve the early critical separations.

Retain injection 8 as the maximum-score benchmark and test a small slope increase from 0.0450 to 0.0458 per minute. This probes whether elution can be shortened slightly without pushing either early critical pair below R 1.5.

Injection 8 already achieves the maximum CRF, and nearby slope changes reveal a tight resolution boundary. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime at a known slope to look for a different fully resolved peak pattern that could support further shortening.

The 25 C run has only one unresolved pair and no time penalty. Raise temperature one step at the same slope to test whether selectivity improves that pair while shortening retention; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Shift the 25 C solvent window upward while preserving its gradient slope to test starting-composition selectivity on the lone unresolved pair. This should also shorten retention; injection 8 remains the established maximum-score method.

With the maximum CRF already secured by injection 8, test a substantially narrower, higher-starting window for a faster alternative. This explores a different selectivity regime rather than making further small changes around the tight resolution boundary.

Return to the promising low-temperature pattern and reduce the slope from injection 13 to spread its lone unresolved pair. The previous last-peak time of 8.41 minutes leaves some margin for a shallower gradient without a time penalty.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.0400 to 0.0389 per minute to lift the remaining R 1.40 pair toward full resolution. The observed slope response suggests this small change can resolve it while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Seek a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 8 by revisiting the higher starting fraction with a shallower slope. Relative to injection 9, this should improve the early R 1.08 pair, while testing whether the later R 1.78 pair retains sufficient resolution.

The high-temperature, higher-starting window shows competing slope requirements, so test an intermediate temperature for a different selectivity balance. This relatively steep gradient targets a faster fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 8 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Lengthen the promising 45 C gradient one step to test whether its two early critical pairs respond favorably to a shallower slope. The 6.45-minute last peak leaves ample room to gain resolution while remaining competitive with injection 8’s elution time.

The limiting early pair at 45 C barely responds to slope, so test a one-step temperature decrease using the faster gradient. Monitor the entire central cluster for selectivity changes, retaining injection 8 as the fully resolved benchmark.

The low-temperature method reached full resolution in injection 16; raise the starting fraction and reduce the slope to seek a faster version. The shallower slope may offset the early-pair resolution loss previously caused by increasing phi0.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 21 to improve its sole limiting pair at R 1.40. This should test a faster low-temperature route to full resolution than injection 16 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting fraction one step and narrow the window to seek a faster version of injection 22. The accompanying slope reduction may preserve the critical early separation; injection 8 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Combine a shallower slope with a one-step temperature increase to improve injection 23’s lone unresolved pair while partly offsetting the added retention time. Retain injection 8 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to 25 C while retaining the shallower gradient: relative to injection 23, this targets its lone unresolved early pair without the late-pair convergence seen at 30 C. Injection 8 remains the fastest demonstrated method achieving the maximum CRF of 1.000.
